newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK Labour sees slower growth,higher deficits.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK Labour sees slower growth,higher deficits.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government, preparing the ground for its first budget next month, said on Thursday that it expected the economy to grow more slowly over the next five years than the ousted Conservatives had forecast.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown also painted a gloomier outlook for public finances, announcing changes to Treasury planning assumptions which are likely to mean higher budget deficits in the coming years.

Brown won the backing of the National Audit Office, an independent watchdog answerable to parliament rather than the government, for his assumption that underlying economic growth will be 2-1/4 percent per year in the coming years.
His Conservative predecessor Kenneth Clarke had predicted medium-term economic growth of 2.5 percent.
"This is the first time that any chancellor has opened up the Treasury's forecasting assumptions to such open and independent scrutiny," Brown said in a statement.
"It means that the budget arithmetic will be based on financial conventions which are open, transparent and accountable."
Brown will present his first budget on July 2. Slower economic growth generally means less tax revenue for the government.

The Treasury said that if its "deliberately cautious" new assumptions about the public finances had been used when the Conservatives presented their last budget in November, budget deficits for the coming five years would all have been forecast higher.

Stressing that it was not making new forecasts, it said the changes would have meant a public sector borrowing requirement (PSBR) in 1997/98 500 million pounds higher than Clarke's forecast of 19 billion pounds ($31 billion).
Borrowing would have been forecast 3.25 billion pounds higher in 1998/99, rising to an extra seven billion in 2001/2002.
Commenting on the Treasury's assumptions, Sir John Bourn, head of the National Audit Office, said:

"While the assumptions adopted by the cancellor are not the only ones which could be reconciled with the evidence, in my opinion they have been arrived at systematically on the basis of the available data and by methods which interpret it in a reasonable way."
Gerard Lyons, an economist at DKB International, said financial markets were relieved because the Audit Office had not found any "black holes" in the public finances.
"Gordon Brown hasn't been let off the hook. He still has very tough public spending plans to adhere to," he said.

The centrepiece of the first Labour budget is expected to be a "windfall" tax on the profits of privatised utility companies, intended to finance a programme to create jobs for 250,000 young and long-term unemployed people.
Some economists also expect Brown to raise taxes on consumption to help to dampen soaring demand that threatens to fuel a resurgence in inflation.
However, he tied his own hands to some extent by promising during the election campaign not to raise income tax rates and to live within strict spending limits set by the Conservatives for two years.

The new assumptions included the expectation that there will be no new privatisation proceeds beyond those already announced and that the new "spend-to-save" programme, intended to boost revenue by reducing tax evasion and waste, would save 4.9 billion pounds rather than the projected 6.7 billion. ($ = 0.609 British Pounds)
